cards.front: Why is biotransformation needed for drug elimination?
cards.back: Most drugs are lipid soluble and would be reabsorbed in renal tubules and persist for a long time. Metabolism converts them into polar, ionised products that kidney and bile can clear.

cards.front: Where does drug metabolism mainly occur, and which other organs contribute?
cards.back: Liver is the main site. Kidney, intestinal wall, lungs and plasma also metabolise drugs.

cards.front: Phase I and phase II biotransformation reactions
cards.text: Phase I reactions include {{oxidation}}, {{reduction}} and {{hydrolysis}}; phase II (synthetic) reactions include {{glucuronidation}}, {{acetylation}}, {{methylation}} and {{sulfation}}.

cards.front: Compare phase I and phase II drug metabolism.
cards.back: Phase I (functionalisation: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) adds or exposes a polar group; the product may be active or inactive. Phase II (conjugation) attaches an endogenous polar molecule, usually giving an inactive, excretable product. Morphine-6-glucuronide is a notable active conjugate.

cards.front: Microsomal vs non-microsomal drug-metabolising enzymes: how do they differ?
cards.back: Microsomal enzymes sit on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mainly of liver (also kidney, gut mucosa, lungs): CYP450 monooxygenases, UGTs, epoxide hydrolases. They carry out most oxidations, reductions, hydrolyses and glucuronidation, and are inducible. Non-microsomal enzymes lie in cytoplasm, mitochondria and plasma (esterases, amidases, some flavoprotein oxidases, most conjugases); they carry out all conjugations except glucuronidation, are not inducible, but many show genetic polymorphism (acetyltransferase, pseudocholinesterase). Hofmann elimination (atracurium) is spontaneous, non-enzymatic breakdown in body fluids.

cards.front: Short note: Prodrugs

points: Inactive compound converted in the body to one or more active metabolites
Greater stability or better bioavailability
Better pharmacokinetic properties, fewer side effects
Selective activation at the site of action (e.g. levodopa crosses the BBB, then forms dopamine in brain)
Levodopa, enalapril, alpha-methyldopa, dipivefrine
Proguanil, prednisone, clopidogrel, bacampicillin, sulfasalazine
Cyclophosphamide, fluorouracil, mercaptopurine, acyclovir
Activation depends on metabolising enzymes, e.g. clopidogrel is a CYP2C19 substrate; codeine needs CYP2D6 to form morphine

cards.front: Which CYP450 isoform metabolises the largest share of drugs, and name two inhibitors of it.
cards.back: CYP3A4/5, which handles roughly half of all drugs. Inhibitors include erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice.

cards.front: Which CYP families handle most drugs, and where do these enzymes sit in the cell?
cards.back: CYP1, CYP2 and CYP3 families mediate about 70-80% of drug metabolism; 57 human CYPs exist. They sit in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (microsomes), mainly in liver, and CYP3A4 is also in the gut wall.

cards.front: CYP inhibitors by isoform
cards.text: {{Erythromycin}}, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice inhibit CYP3A4/5; {{quinidine}}, fluoxetine and paroxetine inhibit CYP2D6; fluconazole and gemfibrozil inhibit CYP2C8/9; {{disulfiram}} and fomepizole inhibit CYP2E1.

cards.front: Which CYP isoform forms the toxic metabolite of paracetamol, and what induces it?
cards.back: CYP2E1 converts paracetamol to the reactive metabolite NAPQI. Chronic alcohol use and isoniazid induce CYP2E1. Glutathione conjugation normally detoxifies NAPQI; depletion leads to hepatotoxicity.

cards.front: Why does codeine fail in CYP2D6 poor metabolisers but cause toxicity in ultrarapid metabolisers?
cards.back: CYP2D6 O-demethylates codeine to morphine, which provides the analgesia. Poor metabolisers form little morphine and get weak pain relief; ultrarapid metabolisers form too much and can be toxic at usual doses.

cards.front: Short note: CYP450 inhibition and drug interactions

points: Azole antifungals and macrolides bind the haem iron of CYP450
Competitive inhibition when two drugs use the same isoenzyme or cofactor
Acts quickly, unlike induction
CYP3A4: erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, verapamil, ritonavir, fluoxetine, grapefruit juice
CYP2D6: quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine
CYP2C9: fluvoxamine, fluconazole, gemfibrozil, trimethoprim; CYP2C19: omeprazole, fluconazole
CYP1A2: fluvoxamine, fluoxetine; CYP2E1: disulfiram, fomepizole
Higher plasma level of the object drug
Higher oral bioavailability of high first-pass drugs
Longer half-life when clearance falls
Toxicity with narrow-margin drugs such as warfarin and phenytoin
Quinidine is a CYP3A4 substrate but inhibits CYP2D6
Low-dose ritonavir boosts other HIV protease inhibitors through CYP3A4 inhibition
Erythromycin or ketoconazole with terfenadine, astemizole or cisapride caused dangerous arrhythmias

cards.front: A patient on simvastatin is started on clarithromycin. Explain the interaction and how it differs when the new drug is an inducer.
cards.back: Simvastatin is a CYP3A4/5 substrate and clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4/5, so simvastatin clearance falls and its level rises. Inhibition acts within hours. An inducer such as rifampin instead lowers levels, but only after days because new enzyme must be synthesised. Drugs with saturable metabolism through a shared isoform are most prone to significant inhibition.

cards.front: Describe the time course of microsomal enzyme induction.
cards.back: Metabolic rate rises about 2 to 4 fold as enzyme synthesis increases. The peak develops over about 4 to 14 days while the inducer is given, and activity returns to baseline over roughly 1 to 3 weeks after withdrawal.

cards.front: CYP450 inducers by isoform
cards.text: Phenobarbitone, phenytoin and carbamazepine induce {{CYP3A}}; rifampin induces {{CYP3A}} and {{CYP2C}}; chronic alcohol and {{isoniazid}} induce {{CYP2E1}}; cigarette smoke induces {{CYP1A}}.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of enzyme induction, and how does its speed compare with inhibition?
cards.back: Inducers increase synthesis of microsomal enzyme protein, mainly CYP450 and UGTs, through nuclear receptors such as PXR and CAR. Because new protein must be made, induction takes days, whereas inhibition acts within hours.

cards.front: Short note: Microsomal enzyme induction

points: Drugs, chemicals and some dietary agents increase synthesis of microsomal enzymes, mainly CYP450 and UGT
Metabolic rate rises about 2 to 4 fold
Peak develops over about 4 to 14 days
Reverses over about 1 to 3 weeks after withdrawal
Phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine (CYP3A)
Rifampin (broad induction)
Chronic alcohol and isoniazid (CYP2E1)
Cigarette smoke and charbroiled meat (CYP1A)
Oral contraceptive failure with rifampin
Loss of nevirapine effect with rifampin; autoinduction by carbamazepine
Increased paracetamol hepatotoxicity
Precipitation of acute intermittent porphyria
Phenobarbitone for congenital non-haemolytic jaundice
Phenytoin in some cases of Cushing syndrome

cards.front: Why can rifampin cause contraceptive failure, and what other consequences does induction have?
cards.back: Rifampin induces CYP3A and other enzymes, so oestrogen of oral contraceptives is inactivated faster and protection is lost. Induction also lowers nevirapine action, lets paracetamol toxicity occur at lower doses (more NAPQI forms), can precipitate acute intermittent porphyria (ALA synthetase derepressed), and speeds clearance of steroids and bilirubin.

cards.front: Contrast the harmful and useful consequences of enzyme induction, with an example of each.
cards.back: Harm: therapeutic failure of drugs cleared by the induced pathway (contraceptive failure, loss of nevirapine action), more toxic metabolite from paracetamol, porphyria, and unpredictable levels when an inducer is used intermittently with anticoagulants, hypoglycaemics, antiepileptics or antihypertensives. Use: phenobarbitone hastens bilirubin clearance in congenital non-haemolytic jaundice, phenytoin in Cushing syndrome, and faster clearance of accumulated poison in chronic poisoning. Autoinduction (carbamazepine, rifampin, nevirapine) means doses may need adjusting with time.

cards.front: What is the most important conjugation pathway in drug metabolism?
cards.back: Glucuronidation by UDP-glucuronosyl transferases (UGTs), acting on -OH and -COOH groups. Glucuronides excreted in bile can be cleaved by gut bacteria and reabsorbed, causing enterohepatic cycling.

cards.front: Acetylation polymorphism
cards.text: N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) polymorphism gives {{slow}} and {{fast}} acetylator phenotypes. Acetylated drugs include {{isoniazid}}, {{hydralazine}}, procainamide, dapsone and sulfonamides; isoniazid neuropathy and hydralazine or procainamide {{lupus}} occur mainly in slow acetylators.

cards.front: List the phase II conjugation reactions with their co-substrates and one drug for each.
cards.back: Glucuronidation (UDP-glucuronic acid; morphine, paracetamol); acetylation (acetyl-CoA; isoniazid, sulfonamides); methylation (methionine; adrenaline, methyldopa); sulfation (sulfotransferases; chloramphenicol, steroids); glutathione conjugation (glutathione-S-transferase; NAPQI); glycine conjugation (salicylates, minor pathway). Conjugates are usually inactive and more polar.

cards.front: What is the enzyme defect in Gilbert syndrome and why does it matter for drugs?
cards.back: UGT1A1 activity is reduced (mainly the UGT1A1*28 promoter variant, with seven TA repeats). UGT1A1 glucuronidation is the rate-limiting step of bilirubin clearance, so drugs that compete for or inhibit it raise bilirubin. Irinotecan's active metabolite SN-38 is inactivated by UGT1A1, so Gilbert patients get higher SN-38 levels and more haematological and GI toxicity.

cards.front: Why are newborns more vulnerable to chloramphenicol and opioids?
cards.back: Neonatal drug-metabolising enzymes are immature: phase I activity reaches adult levels only over the first few months, and glucuronidation and other conjugations are slower. Drugs cleared by these routes accumulate. Species differences show the same principle (cats lack glucuronidation, dogs lack acetylation).

cards.front: Essay: Factors affecting drug metabolism

points: Biotransformation by microsomal (CYP450, UGT) and nonmicrosomal enzymes
Amount and activity of enzymes vary widely between people
CYP2D6 poor and extensive metabolisers; ultrarapid genotype
N-acetyl transferase slow and fast acetylators
Up to about 6-fold variation in metabolic rate among healthy adults
Newborns, especially premature, have low enzyme activity; phase I matures within months
Conjugation takes 3 months or more to reach adult levels
Hepatic function and clearance decline in the elderly
Inhibition: azoles, macrolides, cimetidine, isoniazid
Induction: phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin
Liver disease reduces metabolism and raises oral bioavailability
Smoking, charcoal-grilled food and chronic alcohol alter CYP1A and CYP2E1
Diet can change enzyme levels
Marked interspecies differences in CYP and UGT activity, for example in cats and dogs

cards.front: Define first-pass metabolism and give the formula for oral bioavailability.
cards.back: First-pass (presystemic) metabolism is metabolism of an orally given drug in the gut wall (CYP3A4 is expressed in intestine) and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation. Oral F = fraction absorbed x (1 - hepatic extraction ratio). Sublingual, transdermal and parenteral routes avoid it; rectal avoids it only partly.

cards.front: Define clearance and give its formula.
cards.back: Clearance is the theoretical volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time. CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration.

cards.front: Give the formula for elimination half-life and state how many half-lives are needed for near-complete elimination.
cards.back: t1/2 = 0.693 x V / CL. It is a derived value and is constant only for first-order elimination. About 4 to 5 half-lives are needed for nearly complete elimination (about 94 percent after four).

cards.front: Short note: First-pass (presystemic) metabolism

points: Metabolism of an orally given drug in gut wall and liver before it enters systemic circulation
Hepatic extraction ratio; for high-extraction drugs, hepatic blood flow
Gut-wall CYP3A4 and liver enzyme activity
Genetic variation, enzyme induction or inhibition
High first-pass: propranolol, verapamil, morphine, pethidine, lidocaine, glyceryl trinitrate
Low first-pass: phenobarbitone, tolbutamide, theophylline, diazepam, isosorbide mononitrate
Oral dose much higher than sublingual or parenteral dose
Marked individual variation in oral bioavailability
Bioavailability rises in severe liver disease or with enzyme inhibitors
Sublingual, transdermal or parenteral routes bypass it
F = fraction absorbed x (1 - hepatic extraction ratio)

cards.front: Short note: Clearance of drugs

points: Theoretical volume of plasma from which the drug is completely removed in unit time (analogous to creatinine clearance)
CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration

cards.front: A drug has a high hepatic extraction ratio. Predict its oral dose, bioavailability and levels in severe liver disease or with a competing drug.
cards.back: High extraction means a large oral fraction is lost on first pass, so the oral dose is much higher than the parenteral one and varies widely between individuals. In severe liver disease or when a competing drug occupies the enzyme, extraction falls, oral bioavailability rises and levels can become toxic at the usual dose. Clearance of such drugs follows hepatic blood flow, so a drug that lowers hepatic blood flow slows it (propranolol reduces lidocaine metabolism this way). Routes bypassing first pass (sublingual, transdermal, parenteral) are used instead, e.g. glyceryl trinitrate.

cards.front: Routes of drug excretion
cards.text: Major routes are {{urine}} (kidney), {{bile into faeces}}, {{exhaled air}} for gases and volatile agents, {{saliva and sweat}} (minor), and {{breast milk}}.

cards.front: Renal tubular transport systems
cards.text: The proximal tubule secretes organic {{acids}} through the OAT system and organic {{bases}} through the OCT system; efflux pumps {{P-gp}} and {{MRP2}} sit on the luminal membrane.

cards.front: What are the three processes of renal drug excretion and which matters most?
cards.back: Net excretion = (glomerular filtration + tubular secretion) minus tubular reabsorption. Only unbound drug is filtered (GFR about 120 mL/min). Reabsorption is passive and depends on lipid solubility and ionisation. Tubular secretion is active transport: OAT for acids and OCT for bases.

cards.front: Which drugs are excreted in bile, and why can this prolong their action?
cards.back: Biliary excretion suits conjugates and compounds of molecular weight above about 300, handled by OATP, MRP2, OCT and P-gp. High biliary levels occur with erythromycin, ampicillin, rifampin, tetracycline, oral contraceptives and vecuronium. Gut bacteria can free the drug from its glucuronide so it is reabsorbed (enterohepatic cycling), prolonging action.

cards.front: How does urine pH affect renal excretion of weak acids and weak bases?
cards.back: Only un-ionised drug is reabsorbed from the tubule. Weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine and weak bases in acidic urine. Urine is alkalinised in barbiturate and salicylate poisoning. Acidifying urine could speed excretion of bases (morphine, amphetamine) but is not practised, because acidosis can cause rhabdomyolysis and cardiotoxicity.

cards.front: Explain the effect of probenecid on penicillin and uric acid.
cards.back: Probenecid competes for the OAT organic-acid secretory transporter, so penicillin and ampicillin secretion falls and their action is prolonged. It also blocks urate reabsorption, so uric acid excretion rises (uricosuric); aspirin blocks this uricosuric effect.

cards.front: Essay: Renal excretion of drugs

points: Kidney excretes water-soluble drugs and metabolites
Net excretion = (filtration + secretion) - reabsorption
All non-protein-bound drug is filtered
Depends on plasma protein binding and renal blood flow
GFR is about 120 mL/min and falls after age 50
Passive diffusion of lipid-soluble, un-ionised drug
Ionised drugs stay in the lumen, so urine pH matters
Used for ion trapping in poisoning
Active, through OAT (acids such as penicillin, probenecid, methotrexate) and OCT (bases such as procainamide, cimetidine)
Efflux pumps P-gp and MRP2 on the luminal membrane
Clearance above GFR indicates secretion
Drugs compete for the same carrier (probenecid and penicillin)
Neonates: immature tubular transport, so penicillins and cephalosporins last longer
Elderly and renal failure: lower clearance, so doses need adjustment
Creatinine clearance guides dosing in renal disease
Competition for secretion explains many drug interactions

cards.front: Write the formula for a loading dose and say what it depends on.
cards.back: Loading dose = target plasma concentration x V / F. It depends on volume of distribution and bioavailability, not on clearance or half-life.

cards.front: Short note: Zero-order kinetics of elimination

points: Elimination rate is constant whatever the plasma concentration
A constant amount is eliminated per unit time
Clearance falls as concentration rises
Ethyl alcohol (example in KDT8)
Some drugs move from first-order to zero-order at high doses, so plasma concentration rises disproportionately with dose

cards.front: Define first-order and zero-order elimination with an example of each.
cards.back: First order: rate of elimination is proportional to concentration, so clearance and half-life are constant (most drugs, as enzymes are in excess). Zero order (capacity-limited, Michaelis-Menten): a constant amount is eliminated per unit time, clearance falls as concentration rises and half-life lengthens with dose (ethanol; phenytoin and tolbutamide at higher doses).

cards.front: How is steady-state concentration determined, and what is the plateau principle?
cards.back: Css = dose rate / CL, so for a target Css, dose rate = Css x CL (divide by F for oral). With repeated dosing, drug accumulates until intake equals elimination, and this takes about 4 to 5 half-lives regardless of dose.

cards.front: Short note: Prolongation of drug action

points: Less frequent dosing and better adherence
Smoother plasma levels with fewer peak-related side effects
Round-the-clock control (e.g. overnight)
Slow absorption: sustained or controlled-release oral forms, depot i.m. or s.c. injections, implants, transdermal patches
Highly protein-bound congeners released slowly (e.g. sulfadoxine)
Slower metabolism: chemical change (ethinyl estradiol vs estradiol) or enzyme inhibition (allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine; ritonavir boosting)
Reduced tubular secretion: probenecid with penicillin
Controlled-release forms suit drugs with half-life under 4 h
Not needed for drugs with half-life over 12 h (doxycycline, amlodipine) or for brief-effect drugs (hypnotics)

cards.front: Maintenance dose and steady state: what is the formula, and how long does steady state take?
cards.back: Maintenance dose rate = target Css x CL / F; it depends on clearance (or half-life). With repeated dosing at a fixed rate, drug accumulates until intake equals elimination (plateau principle); steady state is reached in about 4 to 5 half-lives. A loading dose is used when waiting this long is unacceptable (digoxin, chloroquine, amiodarone).

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

points: Narrow-margin drugs: digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides, anticonvulsants, theophylline
Large individual variation: antidepressants, lithium
Toxic drugs in renal failure
Suspected poisoning
Unexplained treatment failure or adherence check
Long-acting drugs: trough steady-state level, just before the next dose
Short-acting drugs: post-absorptive peak, about 1 to 2 h after oral or IM dose
Poisoning: early sample, then repeated to track clearance
Drugs with easily measured effect: antihypertensives, oral anticoagulants, diuretics
Prodrugs such as levodopa
Hit-and-run drugs: reserpine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole
Irreversible drugs such as organophosphates
Revised dose rate = previous dose rate x target Css / measured Css

cards.front: Essay: Zero-order (saturable) versus first-order elimination

points: Elimination = metabolism + excretion
Clearance: volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time
Constant fraction eliminated per unit time; rate proportional to concentration
Clearance and half-life constant; plasma level falls exponentially
Applies to most drugs in the therapeutic range; dose rate and steady-state level linearly related
Constant amount eliminated per unit time once enzymes are saturated (ethyl alcohol)
Rate = Vmax x C / (Km + C)
Clearance falls and half-life lengthens as dose rises
Phenytoin, tolbutamide, theophylline and warfarin shift from first to zero order at higher doses
Plasma concentration rises disproportionately with dose (nonlinear elimination)
Small dose increments can cause toxicity; increase in small steps
Monitor plasma levels (TDM)
Know whether a drug's elimination is saturable before adjusting its dose

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacometrics in individual dosing

points: Dosing tools use pharmacokinetic models built from representative patient populations
Such tools predict an individual's dose from that patient's measured response
Compare predicted pharmacokinetic parameters with the measured concentration
Example: expected clearance 5.5 L/h; a higher measured level gives a revised clearance of 3.5 L/h, so the daily dose is halved
The implicit method is misleading before steady state
At least a week of regular dosing (four half-lives) must pass first

cards.front: Digoxin has a long half-life. Explain how you would start therapy and adjust it after a measured level.
cards.back: Waiting 4 to 5 half-lives to reach steady state is too slow, so a loading dose (target Cp x V / F, depending on V not on CL) is given, then maintenance doses (target Css x CL / F). If a measured level differs from prediction by more than 20%, revise V or CL for that patient (Katzung). Individual Css can be 1/3 to 3 times the population estimate. Digoxin has a low therapeutic index, so therapeutic drug monitoring is useful.

cards.front: What is Hofmann elimination, and why does it make a drug independent of liver and kidney function?
cards.back: Hofmann elimination is inactivation in body fluids by spontaneous molecular rearrangement, with no enzyme involved (e.g. atracurium). Since no organ enzyme or excretory route is needed, its disposal does not depend on hepatic metabolism, unlike enzyme-mediated biotransformation.

cards.front: How can you tell from renal clearance that a drug is actively secreted by the tubules?
cards.back: Glomerular filtration rate is about 120 mL/min, which is the most that filtration alone can clear. If a drug renal clearance is above that, extra removal by tubular secretion (OAT or OCT transporters) must be happening.

cards.front: What is the "boosted" protease inhibitor strategy and which enzyme does it exploit?
cards.back: Low-dose ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, so the levels of co-given protease inhibitors (atazanavir, lopinavir, saquinavir) rise and their doses can be lowered. Inhibition is dose related and can precipitate toxicity of the affected drug.

cards.front: What happens to a high first-pass drug that inhibits its own metabolism, for example verapamil?
cards.back: Oral bioavailability rises and systemic clearance falls, so half-life is prolonged. With chronic dosing verapamil bioavailability nearly doubles for this reason.

cards.front: Name the routes by which drugs and metabolites leave the body.
cards.back: Urine (the main route), bile into faeces, exhaled air, saliva and sweat (minor), and breast milk.

cards.front: What is enterohepatic cycling?
cards.back: A drug or its glucuronide is secreted in bile, split by gut bacteria, and the freed drug is reabsorbed back to the liver. This keeps the drug in the body longer.

cards.front: Why are general anaesthetic gases and alcohol removed by the lungs whatever their lipid solubility?
cards.back: Alveolar transfer depends on the partial pressure of the gas or vapour in blood, not on its lipid solubility.

cards.front: Why does drug excretion into breast milk matter mainly for the infant?
cards.back: Most drugs cross by passive diffusion, so lipid-soluble, weakly protein-bound drugs pass best. The infant receives a small dose, but a lactating mother should take any drug only when essential.

cards.front: Name the drugs or substances excreted in significant amounts in saliva or sweat.
cards.back: Lithium, potassium iodide, rifampin and heavy metals. Saliva and sweat are of minor importance for drug excretion.

cards.front: Why does renal excretion of aminoglycosides parallel GFR?
cards.back: They are highly ionised and poorly lipid-soluble, so tubules do not reabsorb them. Their excretion therefore follows GFR.

cards.front: Essay: Routes of drug excretion, with examples

points: Drugs and metabolites leave the body by urine, bile and faeces, exhaled air, saliva and sweat, and milk
Urine is the most important route for most drugs
Net excretion = (filtration + secretion) minus reabsorption
Only free drug is filtered; GFR about 120 mL/min
Active secretion by OAT (penicillin, probenecid) and OCT (procainamide, cimetidine)
Urine pH traps weak acids and bases; aminoglycosides follow GFR
Active secretion into bile by OATP, MRP2, OCT and P-gp
Molecules above MW 300 favour bile
Enterohepatic cycling prolongs action; e.g. erythromycin, rifampin
Anthracene purgatives and heavy metals go directly into the colon
Volatile anaesthetics and alcohol leave by the lungs
Depends on blood partial pressure, not lipid solubility
Saliva and sweat are minor routes: lithium, potassium iodide, rifampin, heavy metals
Milk: passive diffusion of lipid-soluble drugs; infant exposure is small but drugs should be used in lactation only when essential
Route depends on lipid solubility, ionisation, MW and protein binding
Renal route falls with age and renal failure, so doses are adjusted

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacokinetic parameters governing drug disposition

points: Bioavailability (F), volume of distribution (V) and clearance (CL)
Elimination rate constant k and half-life are derived from V and CL
CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration
First-order: CL constant; zero-order: CL falls as concentration rises
Apparent volume the drug would occupy at plasma concentration
Example: 1000 mg giving 50 mg/L means V = 20 L
Large V (digoxin 6 L/kg) means drug is in tissues, so haemodialysis removes little
k = CL / V
Nearly complete elimination in 4 to 5 half-lives
Css = dose rate / CL
Oral dose rate for target Css = target Css x CL / F
Loading dose = target Cp x V / F (depends only on V); maintenance depends on CL
Penicillin G t1/2 30 min; aspirin 4 h; digoxin 40 h; phenobarbitone 90 h; digitoxin 7 days

cards.front: Which three fundamental parameters govern drug disposition, and what are their symbols?
cards.back: Bioavailability (F), volume of distribution (V) and clearance (CL). F sets how much of the dose arrives, V sets the loading dose, and CL sets the maintenance dose. Half-life and k derive from V and CL.

cards.front: Define apparent volume of distribution and give a worked example.
cards.back: The volume the drug would occupy if spread uniformly at the plasma concentration. 1000 mg giving 50 mg/L means V = 20 L.

cards.front: Why is half-life not an exact index of drug elimination?
cards.back: t1/2 = 0.693 x V / CL depends on two variables that can change independently, so it is a useful guide rather than an exact measure.

cards.front: Why are drugs with a large volume of distribution not easily removed by haemodialysis?
cards.back: Most of the drug is held in tissues, so plasma concentration is low. Examples: digoxin 6 L/kg, propranolol 4 L/kg, morphine 3.5 L/kg.

cards.front: Which parameter governs the maintenance dose rate, and which governs the loading dose?
cards.back: The maintenance dose rate depends on clearance (Css = dose rate / CL), since it must replace what is cleared. The loading dose depends only on volume of distribution (with F), since it fills the distribution volume.

cards.front: Why do drugs with long half-lives need a loading dose?
cards.back: Steady state takes about 4 half-lives, which can be clinically too slow. A loading dose gives a rapid effect and the maintenance dose then sustains it.

cards.front: What is chronokinetics?
cards.back: The kinetic side of chronopharmacology: how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolises and excretes a drug depends on the time of day it is given. Why it matters: the same dose can give different levels, and so different effect and toxicity, at different hours.

cards.front: How does dose timing change toxicity for aminoglycosides and ceftriaxone?
cards.back: Aminoglycosides (amikacin, gentamicin): a single daily dose given in the active day period lowers renal toxicity. Ceftriaxone: night-time dosing lowers toxicity because its total clearance is highest at night.

cards.front: Short note: Chronokinetics

points: Study of how the time of administration alters absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion
One branch of chronopharmacology, alongside chronotherapeutics, chronesthesy, chronergy and chronotoxicology
Master clock sits in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus; light entrains it
Rhythms in gastric acid and pH, motility and emptying, GI blood flow, protein binding, hepatic enzyme activity and blood flow, renal filtration, tubular reabsorption and urinary pH
Antibiotics: efficacy tracks the time concentration stays above MIC; ciprofloxacin is eliminated faster at 10 am than at 10 pm
Antihypertensives: lipophilic drugs give higher Cmax and shorter tmax in the morning; non-dipper patients are dosed once daily in the evening (ACE inhibitors, sartans, calcium antagonists)
Antiepileptic: valproic acid Cmax and absorption rate are higher in the morning
Anticancer: cisplatin renal toxicity is lower with evening dosing
Statins: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors work better in the evening, except atorvastatin
Not every drug shows it, and the timing effects here are reported drug by drug, not for a whole class
Circadian results for an individual drug are not transferable to other drugs of the same class without data
Time doses to gain efficacy or cut toxicity, a principle called chronotherapy
In cancer, time of day can change outcome (chronomodulation), since leukaemic and normal cells keep different rhythms

cards.front: Essay: the cytochrome P450 system - current concept

points: CYP450 enzymes are haem-containing monooxygenases of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum; the reduced enzyme binds carbon monoxide to give a pink complex absorbing near 450 nm, which gives the name
The reaction needs the drug as substrate, molecular oxygen, NADPH and NADPH-P450 reductase; one oxygen atom is inserted into the drug and the other becomes water
They carry out most phase I oxidations, and because one enzyme serves many drugs they are one of the main sources of metabolic drug interactions
Humans have 57 CYP proteins; each name is CYP followed by a family numeral, a subfamily capital letter and an individual numeral, e.g. CYP3A4
The classification rests on amino acid sequence similarity; members of one family have overlapping but distinct substrate specificity
Only families 1, 2 and 3 matter for drugs: they mediate 70-80% of all drug metabolism, and 12 CYPs account for over 90% of the known drug-metabolising reactions
A drug is often a substrate of more than one isoform, so no single enzyme owns its fate

CYP3A4/5 biotransforms nearly 50% of drugs; CYP2D6 about 20%; CYP2C8/9 more than 15 common drugs; CYP2C19 more than 12; CYP1A1/2 and CYP2E1 handle a few substrates each but matter for carcinogen and toxic metabolite formation
As a share of total liver P450 content: CYP3A4 about 30%, CYP2C9 20%, CYP1A2 15%, CYP2E1 10%, CYP2D6 5%, CYP2A6 4%, CYP2B6 1%
CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 together account for roughly 60% of drug metabolism
They sit in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (microsomes) of hepatocytes, and CYP3A4 is also expressed in intestinal mucosa, where it causes first-pass loss, and in kidney

They inactivate most drugs, but also activate prodrugs (codeine to morphine by CYP2D6; cyclophosphamide) and generate toxic metabolites (paracetamol to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine by CYP2E1 and CYP1A2)
CYP3A4/5: terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride, losartan, carbamazepine, diazepam, ritonavir, saquinavir, simvastatin, quinidine, verapamil, lidocaine
CYP2D6: codeine, metoprolol, debrisoquine, tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, haloperidol, risperidone, propafenone, flecainide
CYP2C8/9: phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, tolbutamide, repaglinide, pioglitazone, diclofenac, ibuprofen, losartan
CYP2C19: omeprazole, lansoprazole, phenytoin, diazepam, clopidogrel, citalopram
CYP1A1/2: theophylline, caffeine, paracetamol, carbamazepine
CYP2E1: alcohol, halothane and the toxic metabolite of paracetamol

CYP3A is induced by phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin, glucocorticoids and nevirapine; phenobarbitone and rifampin act on CYP2D6 and CYP2C8/9 too, and carbamazepine and rifampin additionally on CYP2C19 and CYP1A1/2
Isoniazid and chronic alcohol induce CYP2E1; polycyclic hydrocarbons of cigarette smoke, charbroiled meat and omeprazole induce CYP1A

Current mechanism: an inducer is a ligand for a nuclear receptor - pregnane X receptor for CYP3A, constitutive androstane receptor for CYP2B6 and CYP2C9, aryl hydrocarbon receptor for CYP1A - and more enzyme is transcribed
Induction needs new protein: the rate of metabolism rises 2-4 fold, peaks in 4-14 days and returns to basal over 1-3 weeks after the inducer stops

Common inhibitors: the azoles ketoconazole and itraconazole, the macrolides erythromycin and clarithromycin, cimetidine, chloramphenicol, quinidine, disulfiram, diltiazem, verapamil, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, amiodarone, allopurinol, omeprazole, propoxyphene, isoniazid, fluoxetine and the other SSRIs, MAO inhibitors, and ritonavir with the other protease inhibitors

By isoform: CYP3A4 - erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, verapamil, ritonavir, fluoxetine, grapefruit juice; CYP2D6 - quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine; CYP2C8/9 - fluvoxamine, fluconazole, gemfibrozil, trimethoprim; CYP2C19 - omeprazole, fluconazole; CYP1A2 - fluvoxamine, fluoxetine; CYP2E1 - disulfiram, fomepizole
Some bind the haem iron (azoles, macrolides), others compete for the same isoenzyme or cofactor; the effect starts within hours, unlike induction
A drug can be the substrate of one isoform and the inhibitor of another - quinidine is metabolised by CYP3A4 but inhibits CYP2D6

Inhibition raises the level of the object drug and can be fatal with narrow-margin substrates: erythromycin or ketoconazole with terfenadine, astemizole or cisapride produced dangerous ventricular arrhythmias, and quinidine abolishes the analgesic effect of codeine by blocking its conversion to morphine
The boosted protease inhibitor strategy uses low-dose ritonavir purely as a CYP3A4 inhibitor so that other protease inhibitors can be given at lower doses
Induction lowers effect: contraceptive failure and loss of antiretroviral action with rifampin, and paracetamol toxicity at lower doses because more N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine is formed
Autoinduction explains tolerance to carbamazepine, rifampin and nevirapine, and enzyme induction can precipitate acute intermittent porphyria
A drug that inhibits its own metabolism raises its own bioavailability and half-life; verapamil does this, so its oral bioavailability nearly doubles on chronic dosing
Genetic polymorphism of CYP2D6 (poor and ultrarapid metabolizers) and of CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 explains much of the individual and ethnic variation in dose requirement
Species differences in CYP expression make animal toxicity testing an imperfect predictor of human metabolism

The CYP450 system is best seen as a small set of inducible, inhibitable and genetically variable enzymes sitting at the gateway between dose and systemic exposure; knowing which isoform handles a drug predicts its interactions, its first-pass loss and the patient who will accumulate it
